## Results

Adopting a quantitative detection method for profiling Ψ sites in small RNA
To achieve quantitative Ψ detection in small RNA less than 200 nt, we sought to implement the optimized bisulfite chemistry according to our recently published technology, named PRAISE23. However, specific modifications, including m1A and m3C modifications, can block reverse transcription. Inspired by DM-tRNA-seq and DM-Ψ-seq, we aimed to remove these modifications in vitro to improve cDNA synthesis efficiency21,26. We isolated and treated small RNA with AlkB demethylase, and demonstrated that m1A modification nearly disappeared after AlkB treatment using LC-MS detection (Supplementary Fig. 1a). Further integrating ligation-based strand-specific library construction, we established a methodological pipeline for Ψ detection in small RNA (Supplementary Fig. 1b).

We first analyzed read coverage across small RNA transcripts and did not find bias for the 5' or 3' end in the small RNA library (Supplementary Fig. 1c, d). The fractions of different RNA types showed that cytosolic tRNAs (cyto-tRNAs) accounted for 82.15%, mitochondrial tRNAs (mt-tRNAs) for 0.4%, 5S rRNA for 12.2%, and snRNA and snoRNA together for 5.0%, respectively (Fig. 1a). We then employed PRAISE to identify Ψ sites in small RNAs from HEK293T cells. Since cytosolic tRNA was well-known to contain abundant Ψ sites, we globally identified and quantified Ψ sites in the cyto-tRNAs to test the performance of PRAISE in small RNA. In the cyto-tRNAs, 713 and 714 Ψ sites were detected in two technical replicates, respectively, with 705 overlapping Ψ sites, thus demonstrating high reproducibility of PRAISE (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Data 1). Among the 17 non-overlapping sites, the majority of them (12/17) exhibited low modification levels in another replicate (3–5%) (Supplementary Fig. 1e). We further quantified the Ψ level for the individual site based on the deletion signal, and found a high correlation of Ψ modification levels between two technical replicates (R2=0.99) (Fig. 1c). In addition, Ψ sites in mt-tRNAs can also be detected by PRAISE. We identified 31 and 35 Ψ sites in two technical replicates, respectively, with 31 overlapping sites (Supplementary Data 2). Notably, these four non-overlapping sites that had been previously validated by mass spectrometry data27 also exhibited detectable modification signals in another PRAISE technical replicate (Supplementary Data 2). These results demonstrated the high reproducibility of PRAISE for Ψ detection in small RNA.

We compared PRAISE with DM-Ψ-seq, an existing CMC-based technique for detecting Ψ sites in small RNAs21. In general, 577 Ψ sites in cyto-tRNAs identified by PRAISE can overlap with Ψ sites identified by DM-Ψ-seq (Supplementary Fig. 1f). In particular, PRAISE showed its ability to detect Ψ sites in the 3' end of tRNA transcripts due to its ability to enable reverse transcription read through. As shown in Arg-TCG-5 tRNA, DM-Ψ-seq failed to identify Ψ72, whereas PRAISE successfully detected it and revealed a high modification level of 90.3% (Fig. 1d). Additionally, the modification levels of the 577 overlapping sites detected by DM-Ψ-seq and PRAISE showed a low correlation, which was attributed to the lack of quantitative capacity of DM-Ψ-seq (Supplementary Fig. 1g). We also analyzed the total Ψ levels in cyto-tRNA detected by PRAISE and BACS and found that both methods demonstrated good performance in quantitative Ψ detection, comparable to the Ψ/U ratio measured by quantitative LC-MS/MS (Supplementary Fig. 1h). We observed a high overlap ratio, with 510 of 542 (94.1%) BACS sites detected by PRAISE (Supplementary Fig. 1i). For 32 BACS-only Ψ sites, the majority of them exhibited deletion rates greater than 2% but below our 5% cutoff (Supplementary Fig. 1j). In addition, the Ψ levels quantified by PRAISE in HEK293T cells are correlated with those reported by BACS in HeLa cells (Supplementary Fig. 1k). These data indicated that PRAISE is suitable for Ψ detection and quantification in small RNA.

Quantitative Ψ landscapes of cytosolic and mitochondrial tRNA
We next aimed to provide a comprehensive quantitative landscape of Ψ modification in both cyto-tRNAs and mt-tRNAs in HEK293T cells. We first analyzed the distribution and levels of 705 Ψ sites in cyto-tRNAs. Using PRAISE for quantitative profiling at the isodecoder level, we found distinct Ψ distribution patterns across tRNA isodecoders (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Data 1). Although Ψ is known to be the most common modification in total cytosolic tRNAs, the number of Ψ sites per modified tRNA molecule ranges from one to six (Supplementary Data 3). Human Leu-AAG-4 tRNA has the highest number of Ψ sites (six sites). When analyzing Ψ sites in different tRNA regions, we found that Ψ occurs more frequently in the anticodon stem loop (332 sites) compared to the TΨC loop (250 sites) and D loop (90 sites), suggesting that Ψ plays a critical role in translational decoding. Among all Ψ sites, Ψ55 in the TΨC loop is the most conserved modification, being present in all cyto-tRNAs. Following this, Ψ38-40 and Ψ27-28 in the anticodon stem are present in 148 of 198 and 132 of 202 cyto-tRNAs that contain uridine at these positions, respectively. Ψ13 in the D loop is relatively less conserved and is present in several types of cyto-tRNAs. Additionally, specific Ψ modification sites are found in individual tRNA; for instance, Ψ72 is present only in the acceptor stem of tRNA-Arg, Ψ8 is present only in tRNA-Gly, and Ψ20 is present only in the D loop of tRNA-Leu, indicating their particular functional and physiological roles in tRNA.

We further quantified the modification levels of individual Ψ sites using PRAISE. We integrated and displayed the median modification level for each position across modified cyto-tRNAs, based on an alignment of tRNA sequences28 (Fig. 1f). From the results, we observed that the universally conserved modification site, Ψ55, exhibited a very high modification level, reaching a median of 83.4%. Ψ35, located at the center of tRNA-Tyr anticodon, showed a high modification level of 86.9%, which may be crucial for the recognition of UAG stop codon29. Other highly-modified sites included Ψ72, Ψ13, and Ψ39, with median modification levels of 62.9, 62.1, and 59.8%, respectively. In contrast, Ψ30-32 showed moderate modification levels of 16.7, 24.3, and 24.6%, respectively. Altogether, we provided a global overview of Ψ profiles and stoichiometries in human cyto-tRNAs.

We next analyzed the Ψ distribution and levels in mt-tRNAs and found Ψ sites in 17 out of the total 22 mt-tRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 1l, m). Compared to cyto-tRNAs, mt-tRNAs display a distinct Ψ landscape. Notably, the highly-modified Ψ13 and Ψ72 sites common in cyto-tRNAs are absent, while Ψ68, though present in the acceptor stem, shows a low modification level (7.3%). Instead, Ψ27 and Ψ28 are the most conserved and highly-modified sites in mt-tRNAs, with median modification levels of 79.9 and 68.3%, respectively (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Data 2). Ψ39 is also conserved, but its modification level varies widely—for example, 12.9% in mt-tRNA Phe versus 84.3% in mt-tRNA His. Surprisingly, Ψ55, despite being the most conserved site in cyto-tRNAs, is found in only six mt-tRNAs, though its modification levels in mt-tRNA Leu(UUR) and mt-tRNA Ser are as high as 94.5 and 89.2%, respectively. Thus, these results suggested the presence of a differential Ψ installation machinery in mt-tRNAs.

PUS-dependent and dynamic Ψ sites in snRNA and snoRNA
We then profiled the quantitative Ψ landscape in snRNA and snoRNA from HEK293T cells. Notably, Ψ modification levels exhibit distinct patterns between snRNA and snoRNA. In snRNA, 28 Ψ sites were identified, with modification levels clustering primarily around 15 and 60% (Fig. 2a, b and Supplementary Data 4). These sites are predominantly located near the 5' end of snRNA sequences30 (Fig. 2c). In snoRNAs, we identified 37, 31, and 6 Ψ sites in box H/ACA snoRNAs, box C/D snoRNAs, and scaRNAs, respectively, with modification levels mainly clustering around 15% (Fig. 2a, d and Supplementary Data 5). Interestingly, Ψ sites are enriched within functional pockets where snoRNAs engage their RNA targets, consistent with previous findings25. In box H/ACA snoRNAs, Ψ sites are mainly located within the two hairpin regions, while in box C/D snoRNAs, they are primarily found between the D' and C boxes, and between the C' and D boxes (Fig. 2e, f). The results indicated that Ψ modifications may facilitate snoRNA-guided 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation.

DKC1 was reported to install Ψ on rRNA31,32, mRNA23,24, snRNA33, and snoRNA19. We then knocked down DKC1 and performed PRAISE to quantify DKC1 targets in snRNA and snoRNA. We set a threshold of 30.0% decrease in modification levels and identified 12 high-confidence DKC1-dependent sites among 28 Ψ sites in snRNA (Fig. 2g, h and Supplementary Data 4). In snoRNA, three types of snoRNAs showed differential patterns in expression and Ψ levels after DKC1 knockdown. The expression levels of box H/ACA snoRNA and scaRNA decreased significantly, while the expression of box C/D snoRNA remained unchanged (Fig. 2i). This is consistent with a previous study demonstrating that DKC1 deficiency impairs H/ACA snoRNP formation, thereby compromising the stability of box H/ACA snoRNAs19. For scaRNAs, an earlier work has shown that domain-specific mutations in DKC1 can disrupt their 3' end processing34. Notably, the reads coverage in the DKC1 sample was still sufficient for the identification of Ψ sites in snoRNAs, and we identified 22 and 26 DKC1-dependent Ψ sites in box H/ACA and box C/D snoRNAs, respectively (Fig. 2j, k and Supplementary Data 5). The Ψ levels of both box C/D snoRNA and box H/ACA snoRNA decreased significantly, whereas the Ψ levels of scaRNA remained unchanged (Fig. 2j, k).

Only 48 out of 74 Ψ sites in snoRNA are DKC1-dependent (Fig. 2j, k), prompting us to investigate whether stand-alone PUSs also modify snoRNA. In the formation of Ψ sites on mRNA, stand-alone PUS enzymes such as PUS1, PUS7, and TRUB1 serve as the primary modifying enzymes, mediating the majority of Ψ modifications. We speculated that they might have more diverse RNA targets, including snRNA and snoRNAs. To systematically evaluate this possibility, we then performed PRAISE on small RNAs using a comprehensive panel of PUS-deficient HEK293T cell lines, including PUS1−/−, PUS7−/−, TRUB1−/−, RPUSD1−/−, RPUSD2−/−, RPUSD3−/−, PUS1L−/−, PUS7L−/−, and PUS10−/− (details in a later section). In general, DKC1-independent Ψ sites in snRNA and snoRNA remained unaffected in stand-alone PUS knockout cells (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). But interestingly, we found that one specific site, Ψ47 in SNORD65, was modified by PUS7, corresponding to the canonical “UGUAG” motif (Fig. 2l). Re-analysis of the BACS dataset further confirmed that Ψ47 in SNORD65 is PUS7-dependent (Supplementary Fig. 2c). These results demonstrated the presence of both RNA-dependent and RNA-independent mechanisms for Ψ formation in snoRNA.

To further investigate these DKC1-independent sites, we assessed potential snoRNA-guided Ψ installation and found that most snRNA Ψ sites (12/16) match annotated snoRNA guides in established snoRNA–RNA target databases35,36. Moreover, in-silico predictions based on the folding energies between snoRNAs and target sites19 further revealed that many Ψ sites (22/25) within snoRNAs themselves can be paired with specific H/ACA snoRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 2d and Supplementary Data 6). Together, these results suggested that, except for the single PUS7-dependent site, Ψ installation in snRNAs and snoRNAs is largely mediated by snoRNA-guided modification pathways.

Previous studies revealed stress-induced pseudouridylation of U2 snRNA in yeast37. To assess whether dynamics occur in human cells, we subjected HEK293T cells to heat shock and oxidative stress (H₂O₂ treatment). In snRNA, we observed that Ψ89 in U2 showed a significant increase under heat shock, while other snRNA Ψ sites remained unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 2e). Under H₂O₂ treatment, none of the snRNA Ψ sites exhibited significant changes (Supplementary Fig. 2e). In contrast, snoRNAs displayed more pronounced stress-responsive dynamics: four sites significantly decreased following heat shock and two sites decreased under H₂O₂ treatment (Supplementary Fig. 2f). Notably, Ψ95 in SNORA61 was consistently reduced under both conditions, suggesting that this site may represent a conserved stress-responsive Ψ site in human snoRNAs.

tRNA substrates of PUS1
We further investigated the PUS1 substrates in tRNA based on the PRAISE data of WT and PUS1−/− cell lines. In cyto-tRNA, the modification levels of 132 Ψ sites were significantly reduced or completely lost after PUS1 knockout (Fig. 3a, b and Supplementary Data 1). The contexts of these PUS1-dependent Ψ sites exhibited a weak “USR (S=G or C, R=G or A)” motif (Supplementary Fig. 3a). Consistent with previous findings, Ψ27 and Ψ28 were confirmed as major PUS1-dependent sites in cyto-tRNAs, with their median modification levels dropping from 36.8% in WT to 2.5% in PUS1-/- cell lines (Supplementary Data 1). In mt-tRNA, 14 Ψ modification sites were completely absent after PUS1 knockout (Fig. 3c, d and Supplementary Data 2). We found that PUS1 is responsible for the formation of the Ψ27, Ψ28 and Ψ68 sites in mt-tRNAs, with the median level of Ψ27 and Ψ28 sites decreasing from 70.1% in WT to 0.5% in PUS1−/− and the median level of Ψ68 sites decreasing from 7.3% in WT to 0.7% in PUS1−/− (Supplementary Data 1). Furthermore, our results demonstrate that PUS1 knockout does not affect global tRNA expression (Supplementary Fig. 3b, c). These results demonstrated that human PUS1 is a multifunctional enzyme that targets both cyto- and mt-tRNAs, in accordance with previous studies9,10.

Interplay of PUS1 with additional Ψ synthases
During the analysis of PUS1 substrates, we unexpectedly found that the quantitative results showed an interesting pattern. When the modification levels of Ψ27/Ψ28 in cytosolic tRNAs decreased upon PUS1 knockout, the modification levels of nearby Ψ sites in the anticodon stem-loop significantly increased (Fig. 3e). Specifically, the modification level of Ψ28 on Ile-AAT tRNAs decreased from 47.2 to 3.6%, while the level of Ψ30 on the same tRNAs dramatically increased from 19.3 to 56.1% (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Data 1). Similarly, the modification level of Ψ27 on Met-CAT tRNAs significantly decreased from 43.8 to 7.0%, accompanied by an increase in Ψ31 levels from 24.3 to 48.6%. Notably, in Arg-TCT tRNAs, the Ψ28 level decreased from 53.8 to 11.1%, whereas the Ψ36 level increased markedly from 10.7 to 51.4% upon PUS1 knockout (Supplementary Data 1). In addition, after PUS1 knockout, the modification levels of Ψ39 sites also increased when the modification levels of Ψ27/Ψ28 sites decreased within the same tRNA molecule (Fig. 3e). To exclude artificial interplay caused by inefficient labeling of adjacent Ψ sites, we synthesized a spike-in RNA oligo containing two Ψ sites within an Ile-AAT anticodon stem-loop (ASL)–like sequence (Supplementary Fig. 3d). The expected and measured Ψ levels showed excellent agreement, consistent with the single-Ψ spike-in control (Supplementary Fig. 3e). In addition, BACS data further showed the elevated Ψ30 level in Ile-AAT upon PUS1 knockout, providing orthogonal evidence for the interplay (Supplementary Fig. 3f). Together, these results suggested a common interplay within the anticodon stem-loop exists between PUS1 and additional PUSs.

Given that perturbation of one RNA modification enzyme can influence the expression and activity of others38,39, we first analyzed whether PUS1 knockout affects the gene expression of other PUS enzymes. Among the remaining 12 PUSs, the expression levels of most remained unchanged, and only RPUSD1 and RPUSD3, both members of the RluA family, showed a slight upregulation upon PUS1 knockout (Supplementary Fig. 3g). We noted that in PUS1-knockout cells, PUS1 mRNA was not lost despite the loss of protein function, likely because the premature stop mutation did not fully trigger nonsense-mediated RNA decay. Following PUS1 knockout, the most prominent increases in Ψ modification were observed at Ψ30 and Ψ31. tRNAs exhibiting PUS1-dependent increases in Ψ at U30/31 contained a distinct “RGU (R=G or A)” motif, whereas non-interplay tRNAs harbored a “CKU (K=G or U)” motif, indicating that distinct sequence features might account for their differential susceptibility to PUS1-mediated interplay (Supplementary Fig. 3h). Although Ψ31 and Ψ32 have been reported to be catalyzed by RluA family enzymes in yeast40,41, the substrate specificity of the RluA family in humans remains unclear. To further investigate the molecular basis of this interplay, we subsequently analyzed the potential tRNA substrates of human RluA family members.

Characterization of tRNA targets for the human RluA family enzymes
The human RluA family consists of four proteins: RPUSD1, RPUSD2, RPUSD3, and RPUSD4. It has been reported that RPUSD4 mediates pseudouridylation at Ψ3067 of mitochondrial 16S rRNA42; however, the substrates of the other three proteins remain uncharacterized. We generated RPUSD1−/−, RPUSD2−/−, and RPUSD3−/− knockout cell lines using CRISPR/Cas9 in HEK293T cells. The knockout efficiency was confirmed by genomic DNA sequencing, demonstrating efficiencies of ~100.0% for all three cell lines (Supplementary Fig. 4).

We then utilized PRAISE to identify the modification sites and levels of Ψ targets by comparing Ψ sites of wild-type and RPUSD KO cells. Using the stringent criteria (modification level difference >5.0% and reduction in the modification level of Ψ sites >2-fold), we identified 16 RPUSD1-dependent Ψ sites in tRNA-Arg and tRNA-Ile (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Data 7). In contrast, we did not find any confident cytosolic tRNA substrates for RPUSD2 and RPUSD3 proteins (Fig. 4b, c). In mitochondrial tRNA, we identified 3 RPUSD2-dependent Ψ sites, and the modification levels of these sites were nearly abolished (dropped to 0.00%) after RPUSD2 knockout (Fig. 4e and Supplementary Data 7). In contrast, neither RPUSD1 nor RPUSD3 was found to modify Ψ targets in mitochondrial tRNA (Fig. 4d, f). Given that the subcellular localization of PUS proteins can influence their accessibility to potential RNA targets, we used MitoFates43 to predict the mitochondrial localization of the RPUSD proteins. Our results demonstrated mitochondrial targeting signals were absent in the N-terminal of RPUSD1 isoforms (Supplementary Fig. 5a), whereas they were indeed present in the N-terminal of two RPUSD2 isoforms (Supplementary Fig. 5b), suggesting that RPUSD2 is localized in mitochondria. Collectively, RPUSD1 was found to modify the cytosolic Ψ targets and RPUSD2 was found to modify the mitochondrial Ψ targets.

We further analyzed the modification sites and levels of these Ψ targets. Interestingly, in addition to modifying Ψ30 of cyto-tRNAs, RPUSD1 also modified Ψ72 of cyto-tRNA (Fig. 4g). Specifically, the modification level of Ψ30 on cytosolic tRNA-Ile-AAT decreased from 20.0 to 0.0% after RPUSD1 knockout, and the modification level of Ψ72 on cytosolic Arg-TCG tRNA dropped from 58.1 to 0.0% after RPUSD1 knockout (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Fig. 6a). Consequently, we unexpectedly identified Ψ72 as a site specifically catalyzed by RPUSD1, which is entirely distinct from any RluA family homolog in yeast40,41. RPUSD2-dependent Ψ sites are located at U31 and U32 of mitochondrial tRNA (Fig. 4i). The enzyme responsible for Ψ31 modification in mitochondrial tRNAs is highly similar to its yeast homolog Pus940. Notably, our results revealed that RPUSD3 has no targets on any cyto-tRNAs or mt-tRNAs, indicating it lacks catalytic activity due to the absence of a critical aspartate residue2. Furthermore, we investigated whether these knockouts or targeted Ψ sites affected tRNA expression. Analysis revealed that there is no significant impact on the global expression levels of either cyto- or mt-tRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 6b, c). The impact of Ψ targets modified by the human RluA family in tRNA biogenesis and translational fidelity warrants further investigation.

Interplay of RPUSD1 and PUS1
The results showed that RPUSD3 does not act on substrates in either cytosolic or mitochondrial tRNAs; thus, the observed increase in Ψ30 and Ψ31 sites following PUS1 knockout was not caused by altered RPUSD3 expression. Interestingly, upon RPUSD1 knockout, in addition to a significant reduction in Ψ30 on its tRNA substrate Ile-AAT, we observed a notable increase in the adjacent modification site, Ψ28, on the same tRNA molecule (Fig. 4j). Specifically, our quantitative data showed that the Ψ level of Ψ28 increased by more than 30% following RPUSD1 knockout. To determine whether this effect was due to upregulated PUS1 expression leading to increased modification levels of its targets, we examined PUS1 expression levels. However, PUS1 expression remained unchanged after RPUSD1 knockout (Supplementary Fig. 6d), indicating that the observed changes in modification levels were not attributable to altered PUS1 expression. Given the interplay between adjacent Ψ sites, we speculate that this phenomenon may arise from steric hindrance among different PUS enzymes and may reflect a broader regulatory mechanism involving multiple Ψ-modifying enzymes within the anticodon stem-loop.

To assess whether PUS interplay depends on the catalytic activity of PUS1, we performed rescue experiments in PUS1 knockout cells using wild-type PUS1 or the catalytic-dead D118A mutant11 and the disease-associated nonsense variant E192X10 (Supplementary Fig. 7a–e). Specifically, PUS1 knockout HEK293T cells were transfected with constructs encoding wild-type human PUS1 isoform 2 or the corresponding D118A or E192X mutant proteins. PRAISE sequencing showed that wild-type PUS1 successfully restored the Ψ28 modification and reduced the elevated interplay-associated Ψ30 level in Ile-AAT tRNA. In contrast, neither D118A nor E192X rescued Ψ28 modification or the interaction with Ψ30 (Supplementary Fig. 7f–h). These results indicate that loss of catalytic activity, whether caused by mutation of the catalytic residue or by pathogenic truncation, might abolish the ability of PUS1 to mediate PUS interplay.

The interplay of PUS7 with PUS1 and PUS3
Since Ψ35 in tRNA has been reported as a PUS7 target44, we then aimed to explore potential interplays between tRNA modification enzymes PUS1 and PUS7. To this end, we applied PRAISE to the PUS7−/− cell line to identify its substrate sites. We first found that PUS7 knockout does not affect the expression of other PUS enzymes (Supplementary Fig. 8a), nor does it alter the global expression levels of cytosolic or mitochondrial tRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 8b, c). Then we identified 100 PUS7-dependent Ψ sites in cytosolic tRNAs (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Data 1). Their modification levels decreased significantly by >50%, and their contexts were consistent with the well-known PUS7 motif “UGUAG” (Fig. 5b, c). We also found that PUS7 mainly mediated the formation of Ψ13, Ψ20b, and Ψ50 in 83 cytosolic tRNAs (Fig. 5d). Additionally, we did not identify any Ψ modification sites in mt-tRNAs, indicating the absence of PUS7’s localization and catalytic activity in the mitochondria.

After PUS7 knockout, we observed that the levels of Ψ28 in Arg-TCT tRNAs significantly increased from 55.4 to 70.1%, while its target site Ψ36 decreased significantly from 11.2 to 0.0% (Fig. 5e). Conversely, in PUS1−/− cell line, the modification levels at Ψ28 sites decreased from 55.4 to 10.8%, while the modification levels at Ψ36 sites increased from 11.2 to 56.6%. These results provide evidence for the interplay between PUS1 and PUS7 in the anticodon stem-loop region. We then analyzed the changes in the levels of nearby targeted Ψ sites and found that the modification levels of Ψ35 sites in Tyr-GTA tRNA isoacceptors decreased from 87.7 to 0.0%, while the modification levels of Ψ39 sites increased from 13.0 to 62.8% (Fig. 5d, f). Since Ψ39 is located in the anticodon stem-loop and has been shown to be catalyzed by PUS345, these results suggest an interplay between PUS7 and PUS3 in the anticodon loop of cyto-tRNAs. tRNAs carrying U39 were grouped into PUS1- or PUS7-targeted and non-targeted sets. In both PUS1 and PUS7 knockout cells, Ψ39 increased only in the respective targeted tRNAs, while non-targeted tRNAs showed no significant change (Supplementary Fig. 8d–g). These results indicated that the observed Ψ39 elevation occurs specifically at PUS-dependent substrate sites rather than through a global increase effect.

To further investigate whether the interplay among PUSs occurs at other positions of cyto-tRNA, we applied PRAISE to the generated TRUB1−/− cell line, where TRUB1 catalyzes the highly-modified Ψ55 sites in the TΨC loop of tRNA. We first detected that TRUB1 knockout did not affect the expression of other PUSs (Supplementary Fig. 9a). Using the criteria mentioned above, a total of 28 TRUB1-dependent sites were identified (Supplementary Fig. 9b and Supplementary Data 1). These sites were primarily localized at Ψ55, and their context conformed to the TRUB1 motif “GUUCNA” (Supplementary Fig. 9c, d). Compared to PUS1-dependent and PUS7-dependent sites, the reduction in modification levels of TRUB1-dependent sites was less pronounced. To investigate the potential redundancy between TRUB1 and PUS10 in cytosolic tRNAs46,47, we utilized a previously generated PUS10−/− HEK293T cell line21 and performed PRAISE analysis on small RNAs. Consistent with our earlier CMC-based findings, Ψ54 sites in tRNA were completely abolished upon PUS10 knockout. Moreover, 21 Ψ55 sites showed substantial decreases in the PUS10-/- cells, including those in Ala-AGC, Val-AAC, Val-TAC, and Val-CAC tRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 9e). Notably, we also identified an additional set of 14 Ψ55 sites that exhibited modest reductions and were affected by both PUS10 and TRUB1 knockout (Supplementary Fig. 9f). Together, these results revealed functional redundancy between PUS10 and TRUB1 at cytosolic tRNA Ψ55 sites.

In contrast to cytosolic tRNA, we identified 6 TRUB1-dependent sites, all located at Ψ55, in mitochondrial tRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 9g and Supplementary Data 1), and their modification levels were eliminated upon TRUB1 knockout (Supplementary Fig. 9h). These findings excluded Ψ55 synthase activity of TRUB247. Consistent with its mitochondrial role48, immunofluorescence staining in HeLa cells showed that TRUB2 is exclusively localized to mitochondria (Supplementary Fig. 10a), raising the possibility that TRUB2 may contribute to mitochondrial function via non-catalytic mechanisms. We found that TRUB1 knockout did not affect the expression of cyto- and mt-tRNAs, which confirmed that the change of Ψ level was not caused by tRNA expression (Supplementary Fig. 9i, j). Meanwhile, although the modification level of Ψ55 on cyto-tRNA and mt-tRNA decreased, the modification level of nearby sites did not significantly change (Supplementary Fig. 9d). Therefore, the results suggested that the interplay among different PUSs in tRNA primarily occurs in the anticodon stem-loop region.

tRNA substrates for PUS1L and PUS7L
To further expand the tRNA Ψ landscape, we generated knockout HEK293T cells for stand-alone PUS1L and PUS7L and performed PRAISE sequencing to identify their Ψ substrates. Remarkably, PUS1L knockout eliminated all seven Ψ39/40 sites in mitochondrial tRNAs while not significantly influencing Ψ sites in cyto-tRNAs, indicating that PUS1L exclusively modifies mt-tRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 10b and Supplementary Data 1 and 2). Immunofluorescence analysis also showed its mitochondrial localization (Supplementary Fig. 10c, d). In contrast, PUS7L knockout led to a pronounced reduction in 25 Ψ sites (Supplementary Fig. 10e, f). These PUS7L-dependent sites were restricted to type II tRNAs, which are defined by an extended variable loop. The affected tRNAs included Ser-GCT, Leu-AAG, Leu-CAA, and Leu-TAG, and all Ψ sites were located within the variable loop region (Supplementary Data 1). Together, these results indicated that PUS1L and PUS7L display substrate specificity entirely distinct from their paralogs, PUS1 and PUS7, suggesting that they may have specialized functions that warrant further investigation.

## Methods

Cell culture
HEK293T cells were maintained in DMEM medium (Corning) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco), 1% GlutaMAX (Gibco), and 0.5% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco) at 37°C with 5% CO2. Cells within passage 6 were used for experiments. Stress conditions were applied as follows: heat shock was induced by incubating cells at 43°C for 2 h, followed by a 6 h recovery at 37°C, and oxidative stress was induced by treating cells with medium containing 1 mM H₂O₂ (Sigma) for 1 h.

Generation of stable knockdown and CRISPR knockout cell lines
The shRNA targeting DKC1 (TRCN0000010325) was designed and transfected into HEK293T cells as described in our previous study23. PUS1, PUS7, TRUB1, PUS10 KO in HEK293T cells were generated by previous studies17,21,23,61. RPUSD1, RPUSD2, RPUSD3, PUS1L, and PUS7L KO HEK293T cells were newly generated by CRISPR–Cas9 technology62. sgRNA sequences were listed as follows:
RPUSD1-sgRNA: CCGGCAGCGCGTACAGGTGC
RPUSD2-sgRNA: AAGGTCGTAGCGCCAATGTC
RPUSD3-sgRNA: CTCCAGAACCGGCCCAAAAC
PUS1L-sgRNA: AGGCCCTCAACACACACCTG
PUS7L-sgRNA: CTGAACCAGACTGATGATTT

Plasmid construction and cell transfection in rescue experiments
Wild-type human PUS1 isoform 2 was cloned from cDNA into the pcDNA3.1(+) vector (Invitrogen). Using this plasmid as a template, we generated two mutant variants: a premature termination mutant10 (PUS1-iso2 E192X) and a catalytically inactive mutant11 (PUS1-iso2 D118A). Site-directed mutagenesis was performed using the Mut Express II Fast Mutagenesis Kit V2 (Vazyme) with the following primers. Plasmids were transfected into PUS1-KO HEK293T cells using Lipofectamine LTX with Plus™ Reagent (Invitrogen). Cells were harvested 48 h post-transfection for RNA and protein extraction.
PUS1-iso2 E192X_F primer: TCAGGTTAGACCTACCGCCTGAGCGCCGAGA
PUS1-iso2 E192X_R primer: GGTAGGTCTAATCCTGAACGTCCCGGTCCTTG
PUS1-iso2 D118A_F primer: GACAGCCAAGGGTGTGTCCGCAGCCGGCCAGG
PUS1-iso2 D118A_R primer: ACACACCCTTGGCTGTCCGGGCGCAGCGCTGG

Small RNA purification
Total RNA was extracted with TRIzol (Life technologies) followed by isopropanol precipitation, according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Invitrogen). The resulting total RNA was treated with DNase I (NEB) to avoid DNA contamination. Size selection was performed using MEGAclear Transcription Clean-Up Kit (Ambion) to deplete large RNA. The small RNA fraction was subsequently purified by ethanol precipitation.

PRAISE for small RNA
About 300 ng of small RNA from each technical replicate was denatured and demethylated by incubating with 2× molar ratio of wild-type AlkB, and subsequently recovered through phenol-chloroform extraction and ethanol precipitation. About 100 ng demethylated small RNA was transferred into a new nuclease-free tube and used as “untreated” and stored at −80°C. Sulfite/bisulfite reagent was freshly prepared by dissolving 2.58 g of potassium sulfite (Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.30 g of sodium bisulfite (Sigma-Aldrich) in 8 ml RNase-free water. The 100 mM hydroquinone was prepared freshly by adding 11.01 mg of hydroquinone (Sigma-Aldrich) to 1 ml of RNase-free water. For sulfite/bisulfite treatment, 5 µl of RNA was mixed with 50 µl of sulfite reaction, which is a 100:1 mixture of sulfite/bisulfite reagent and 100 mM hydroquinone, and subjected to heat incubation at 70°C for 5 h. The reaction mixture was desalted by twice passing through Micro Bio-spin 6 chromatography columns (Bio-Rad). Desalted RNA was then incubated with an equal volume of 1 M Tris-HCl (pH 9.0) at 75°C for 30 min. The reaction was then immediately stopped by chilling on ice and ethanol precipitation.

After ethanol precipitation, “treated” and “untreated” small RNA samples were subjected to library construction according to the eCLIP protocol with several modifications63. RNA samples were dephosphorylated with T4 PNK (NEB). 3' adapter (5'-rApp-AGATCGGAAGAGCGTCGTG-C3spacer-3') was ligated using T4 RNA Ligase 2, truncated KQ (NEB) at 25°C for 2 h. The excess adapter was digested using 5' deadenylase and RecJf (NEB). RNA was reverse transcribed using Maxima H minus (Invitrogen) and RT primer (ACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT), following by RNase H treatment. 5' linker (5Phos-NNNNNNNNNNAGATCGGAAGAGCACACGTCTG-3SpC3) ligation was performed with T4 RNA Ligase 1, High Concentration (NEB). The ligated cDNA was purified using silane beads and then subjected to PCR amplification using PCR primers: 5'-AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACTCTTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT-3', 5'-CAAGCAGAAGACGGCATACGAGATXXXXXXGTGACTGGAGTTCAGACGTGTGCTCTTCCGATC-3' (XXXXXX represents index sequence). PCR products were purified using 8% native-PAGE gel. The libraries were sequenced on Illumina HiSeq X10 with a paired-end 2×150 bp read length.

Preprocessing of raw reads
The PRAISE library construction enables reads 2 to retain the original RNA direction, so only reads 2 was used for analysis in this study. First, Cutadapt (version 4.8)64 was used to remove the adapter and perform quality control of the sequencing reads. The key parameters are: cutadapt -j 28 --times 1 -e 0.1 -O 3 --quality-cutoff 25 -m 55. After that, based on the 10 bp unique molecular identifier (UMI) at the 5' end of reads 2, the duplicated sequences were removed by Seqkit (version 0.13.2)65. The key parameters are: seqkit rmdup -s. Finally, the 10 bp UMI was extracted by umi_tools (version 1.0.0)66. The key parameters are: umi_tools extract --extract-method=string --bc-pattern=NNNNNNNNNN. In addition, the library construction added 6 bp bases at the 3' end of insertion, which was also removed by umi_tools (version 1.0.0). The key parameters are: umi_tools extract --extract-method=string --3prime --bc-pattern=NNNNNN.

Cleaned reads alignment of PRAISE
Human cytosolic tRNAs reference (GRCh38) was retrieved from the database GtRNAdb67. Only non-redundant tRNA sequences were retained, and a “CCA” sequence was added to the 3' end of each tRNA. The mitochondrial tRNAs reference was downloaded from NCBI. Other small RNA references (snRNA, snoRNA, microRNA, yRNA, and <200 nt rRNAs) originated from the human transcriptome (GRCh38). The snRNA and snoRNA entries were streamlined to only one representative sequence per type.

A two-step strategy was implemented to ensure the alignment accuracy: (1) BWA-MEM was used to align the cleaned reads to the reference transcriptome of total small RNAs. The key parameter is: bwa mem -Y. (2) A custom Python program was used to realign the mapped reads from the previous step. This program was based on biopython and adopted an optimized scoring matrix to precisely resolve deletion signals. The key parameters were: python realignment.py –fast -ms 4.8. After that, the custom Python program remove_end_signal.py was used to remove 3'-end deletion signals to reduce false-positive sites. Samtools (v1.14) was used to convert the BAM file into an mpileup format file68. The key parameters are: samtools mpileup -d 1500000 -BQ 0 --ff UNMAP,QCFAIL -aa. Finally, the information in the mpileup file was counted and converted into a BMAT format file for subsequent signal identification.

Identification of Ψ signal
Ψ site identification required three criteria: (1) For each T site, a 2×2 contingency table was constructed using deletion counts and non-deletion counts (total counts - deletion counts) from treated and untreated samples. Significant inter-group differences were assessed by χ² or Fisher’s exact test. The p value is required to be <0.0001; (2) The deletion rate was defined as follows: deletion counts/total counts. The deletion rate difference between treated and untreated samples is required to be >5%. (3) Ψ sites must be detected in both technical replicates. The mean detected signal between replicates was reported as the final signal of each Ψ site.

Identification of PUS-dependent Ψ sites in small RNA
To identify PUS-dependent sites, the final Ψ list in WT samples was taken as a reference. The decreasing rate of deletion signal in tRNA between PUS-KO samples and WT samples is required to be >50%. The decreasing rates of deletion signal in snRNA and snoRNA between DKC1-KD samples and WT samples are required to be >30%. The total coverage of PUS-dependent sites is required to be >10 reads.

Analysis of tRNA expression
Adapter trimming and quality control of raw reads were performed using Cutadapt (version 4.8). The cleaned reads were mapped to the tRNA reference (GRCh38) using BWA-MEM with default parameters. The mapped reads were processed using samtools (v1.14). RNA coverage was quantified using pysam. RNAs with low technical reproducibility were discarded. The criteria is: log2 fold change (coverage of technical replicate 1/coverage of technical replicate 2) >1. tRNA expression levels were calculated using RPM.

Analysis of RNA expression
Cutadapt (version 4.8) was used for quality control and adapter trimming of raw reads. The cleaned reads were mapped to the reference transcriptome (GRChg38) using Hisat2 with default parameters69. Mapped reads were processed by samtools (v1.14). Gene coverage was quantified by featureCounts. The key parameters are: featureCounts -t exon -g gene_id. RNAs with low technical reproducibility were discarded. The criteria is: log2 fold change (coverage of technical replicate 1/coverage of technical replicate 2) >1. The expression of PUSs was calculated by FPKM.

Motif analysis, correlation analysis, and statistics analysis
We extracted the upstream and downstream sequences of the target site, and then ggseqlogo in R (v. 4.3.1) was used for Motif visualization. The data in this study were continuous data, so the statistical parameter in the correlation analysis was the Pearson correlation coefficient. The statistical tests used in this study mainly included the two-sided Student’s t-test and the Wilcox rank-sum test. The two-sided Student’s t-test was used when the data conformed to the normal distribution and the data variance was homogeneous; otherwise, the Wilcox nonparametric rank-sum test was used. Error bars represent mean ± s.d.

Target prediction on snRNA and snoRNA
We performed an in-silico target prediction analysis based on the snoRNA database36. For each pseudouridine site detected, a 21-nt window containing 10 nt upstream and downstream of the modified position was extracted to generate the target set. The 3' and 5' catalytic hairpin regions of all H/ACA box snoRNAs were obtained using RNAfold (2.7.0) from the ViennaRNA Package70 and used as the snoRNA query library. We then used RNAsnoop (2.7.0) from the ViennaRNA Package to generate specific binding models of the query library and target set. The key parameters are: RNAsnoop -s snoRNA query library -t target set -d 2. We employed filtering criteria in RNAsnoop to minimize false positives: (1) ≥4 base pairs in the 5' duplex, (2) ≥4 base pairs in the 3' duplex, and (3) a total predicted free energy <–10 kcal/mol.

### Reviewer 1

This study comprehensively profiled pseudouridine (Ψ) modifications in small RNAs—including cytosolic and mitochondrial
tRNAs, snRNAs, and snoRNAs—in HEK293T cells using the quantitative Ψ detection method known as PRAISE. As a
result, the authors newly identified the RNA substrates and corresponding modification sites for multiple pseudouridine
synthases (PUSs). Furthermore, they demonstrated crosstalk among multiple PUS enzymes in the anticodon stem-loop
region of tRNAs, whereby these enzymes influence each other's modification activity. These findings represent the first
comprehensive, quantitative, and high-resolution dataset of Ψ modifications and mark a significant milestone in the field of
RNA modification research. Below are several points for consideration.
Adding a discussion on the physiological relevance of the observed interplay among PUS enzymes would greatly enhance
the manuscript. For instance, could such interplay reflect a compensatory mechanism that maintains tRNA functionality in
response to the loss of specific modifications?
In PUS1 and PUS7 knockout cells, increased Ψ modification at position 39 was observed in many tRNAs that contain the
respective target sites for these enzymes. Do similar changes also occur in tRNAs that do not carry these target sites?
Discussing this point would be important for understanding potential interactions among PUS enzymes.
To provide a more comprehensive understanding, it would be valuable to present data on the Ψ modification sites and their
levels in snRNAs and snoRNAs in RPUSD1–3 knockout cells.
It is useful to summarize all the data (Ψ position, tRNA species, and dependency on each enzyme) in a single table (e.g., an
Excel sheet).
Other comments
The data indicate that Ψ8 is present only in Gly-GCC, but Reference 14 claims that Ψ8 is found in fragments derived from
Ala, Cys, and Val as well. How do the authors reconcile this discrepancy?

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript entitled “Quantitative analysis of small RNA pseudouridylation reveals interplay of PUS enzymes in tRNA
anticodon stem-loop”, Liu et al adapted their original PRAISE method to small RNA Ψ profiling by incorporating AlkB
demethylation to remove the methylation of several tRNA modifications to improve the readthrough in RT reaction, enabling
quantitative and site-specific profiling of Ψs in small RNA. The method worked very well for quantitative profiling the Ψ sites
in small RNA including tRNA, snRNA and snoRNA. By perturbing seven PUS enzymes using stable knockdown or
knockout cell lines, the authors made interesting discoveries including: (1) pseudouridylation of snoRNAs can be mediated
other stand-alone enzyme PUS7 in addition to DKC1; (2) quantification of the Ψ fractions in KO and WT samples not only
allow the assignment of the tRNA substrates of individual PUS enzyme, but also reveal unexpected interplay among PUS
enzymes in shaping Ψ patterns within the ASL; and (3) for the first time the tRNA targets of the human RluA family were
determined the human tRNA targets which differs from that of its yeast counterparts. The manuscript was written very clearly
and the evidence they showed are adequate to support their conclusions. Their finding will definitely benefit more functional
studies of Ψ and PUS enzymes. Therefore, this reviewer supports its publication in Nature Communications after minor
revision.
The following are some minor comments:
Line 107-108, “However, specific modifications, including m1A and m3C
modifications, can block reverse transcription”. Besides m1A and m3C, how about other modifications in tRNA such as m1G
and m22G? Can these modifications also block RT reactions? Can these RNA modifications be demethylated by AlkB
treatment?
Line 118-9: “rRNA accounted for 12.3%”. The small RNA fraction should not have much rRNA contamination, is there some
rRNA degradation in the course of small RNA purifications?
Line 123 “In the cyto-tRNAs, 713 and 714 Ψ sites were detected in two technical replicates, respectively, with 705
overlapping Ψ sites, thus demonstrating high reproducibility…” it would be nice to describe the quality of these libraries,
such as the mapping ratio, deduplication rate, insert sizes, and the criteria to call these sites. In addition, for the non-
overlapped Ψ sites, are their fractions lower in general than the detected sites? What might be the reasons why these sites
failed to overlap?
Line 174-175 “modification level, reaching a median of 83.4%. Ψ35, located at the center of tRNA-Tyr anticodon, showed a
high modification level of 86.9%”. The detected modification level is calculated based on the deletion rate and the calibration
curves?
Line 213 “12 high-confidence DKC1-dependent sites among 28 Ψ sites in snRNA”, for the other 16 Ψ sites in snRNA, any of
them is sensitive to the KO of the other PUS enzymes?
Line 411-414, “facilitate characterization of additional PUS enzymes, such as PUS1L and PUS7L, enabling comprehensive
mapping of tRNA Ψ modifications and advancing our understanding of PUS-mediated Ψ formation.” Is there any specific
reason why the authors don’t include the KO of PUS1L and PUS7L in this study?

### Reviewer 3

Major comments:
- The authors performed a comprehensive analysis of pseudouridylation in human tRNAs as well as other small RNAs
including snoRNAs and snRNAs. The data demonstrate all of the positions of pseudouridylation, while quantifying levels
using their previously established method, named PRAISE. They were also able to assign many of the sites to specific
pseudouridine synthases through analysis of cells with knockdown or knockouts of 7 different pseudouridine synthases. The
innovation derives primarily from the large scale of data, and this work will serve as a very useful resource for the community
studying RNA modifications in tRNAs, snRNAs, and snoRNAs. The authors do highlight some novel findings, including a
snoRNA pseudouridine site not catalyzed by DKC1 but by “stand-alone” synthase PUS7, as well as new examples of
apparent interplay between different pseudouridines in the anticodon stem/loop, in which loss of one site can lead to either
increases or decreases of other sites catalyzed by other enzymes. These examples are limited in comparison to the rest of
the data presented, however, they are not orthogonally validated by another method and are not considered in regard to
hypotheses or models that could be tested, which would have extended their significance for the field. This work represents
a great resource for the field, but alone does not present a significant new understanding of tRNA biology, although the data
have this potential if extended through further analysis or discussion.
- This work showcases the potential of PRAISE to establish the record of where pseudouridine is and at what levels
quantitatively. A limitation is that information about other modifications is not recorded. This may not influence interpretation
of analysis of snoRNAs and snRNAs, because those RNAs are not known to contain a wide variety of modifications, at high
density. But for tRNAs, there is a lot of lost information in not considering how loss of pseudouridine may influence other
modifications. For example, several examples are known in which loss of pseudouridine in tRNA at specific sites can affect
other modifications (Porat 2025 for review). While it remains challenging to record this information, it is suggested that the
authors nonetheless acknowledge this limitation of the approach in the text, and discuss the possibility that some of the
interplay that they observe is “indirect” (in that it is happening through one pseudouridine influencing another modification,
which is in turn influencing a different pseudouridine site). To summarize, due to the complexity of the tRNA modification
landscape, it is difficult to draw conclusions for interplay between modifications when only examining one type out of more
than two dozen possibilities in tRNA.
- The quantitative analysis of pseudouridylation site modification is impressive, but sometimes other aspects of quantification
need improvement. For example, in the analysis presented in lines 227–236, it describes how 48/73 sites are DKC1-
dependent. Then after analysis of three mutants, it is concluded that one site is PUS7-dependent. Was this site one of the 25
that were not DKC1-dependent? Presumably? But what about the other 24? Are there any ideas for what those could be
catalyzed by? Given that this result was stated in the abstract, there needs to be a more quantitative description of the
number of sites in snoRNAs that are DKC1-dependent, and the number of new sites that have been revealed to be
depended on a stand-alone synthetase, which from this study appears to be one (SNORD65). Moreover, because of the
apparent significance of this result—it is mentioned in the abstract—the authors can consider whether they would like to
demonstrate it by an orthogonal approach. Given that the entire study basically consists of PRAISE assays, this type of
result is of the type that may most benefit from an orthogonal validation.
- The description of changes on mt-tRNAs resulting from the absence of a TRUB1 were interesting but would benefit from
the addition of a description of the possible role of TRUB2. It would also be beneficial to know whether the cytosolic
tRNAs that were not changed by TRUB1 deletion lacked the motif described in line 275. Or differed in other features. The fact that a
relatively small number of these isoacceptors were affected, and to incomplete levels is interesting, and more discussion of
PUS10 vs. TRUB1 would improve impact of understanding these interesting these results.
- In the case where there is “interplay” between different modified sites in the anticodon loop, how is “labeling efficiency” of a
given site affected when there is a strong decrease in a neighboring site? Presentation of data that would refute such an
artifactual model for changes would be appreciated.
- Pathogenic variants of PUS1 and PUS7 are included in the introduction, but not in the discussion. Given that this study
found several examples where PUS1 or PUS7 catalyzed pseudouridine sites impact other sites, it would be reasonable to
speculate how these interactions may be involved in a disease mechanism. In the case of PUS1 disease variants, several
are known to have a reduction/loss of catalytic activity, which could possibly cause altered interactions with other
pseudouridine sites compared to a PUS1 knockout. In summary, connecting the findings of this study to pathogenic variants
would emphasize the broader importance of the results.
- The paper title and results section are centered on tRNA. The section on snoRNA and snRNA, while adding value to the
study, feels out of place. It is suggested to move this section to the end to maintain the focus on tRNA that appears to be the
intent of the authors. And to reframe the study as a focus on tRNA, but that additional analyses of these other classes of RNA
added further novelty to the study.
- The analysis of mRNA and tRNA expression are not sufficiently explained. Why were these done? How do they facilitate
interpretation of the PRAISE data? Some examples from the literature should be provided that defend the idea that loss of
one PUS enzyme or other RNA modification enzyme has been shown to lead to changes in another enzyme, and to a
significant enough degree that it would affect the activity of that second enzyme. Otherwise, this analysis seems to yield
limited value for the space that it occupies, and without further discussion to emphasize its importance.
- A major focus of this study is the interplay between pseudouridine sites in the anticodon stem-loop, of which they found
several interesting examples. However, there are many tRNAs that are modified by PUS1 and do not have an increase in Ψ
levels at U30/31 (Fig. 3e). Are there any shared features (i.e. tRNA sequence, structure, etc.) that may influence whether an
interaction between Ψ27/28 and Ψ30/31 is present? In lines 386-387, the authors state that interactions between PUSs
primarily occurs in the anticodon stem-loop, which is somewhat contradictory to the data presented in Fig. 3e and 5d that
show several examples of interactions between Ψ sites in other regions of the tRNA. The mechanisms proposed in lines
429-439 could benefit from additional references to structural/biochemical literature on PUSs.
- Some of the figure legends are very short and do not provide the complete information necessary to interpret the plot. For
example, there is insufficient explanation of the heat maps shown in 1e, 3e and 5d/f. For example, it is not clear the order
that the isodecoders are labeled, and in general there just needs to be more detail in how these are presented.
Minor comments:
- Figure 3F, 4J: the labels caused some confusion. Is this a standard nomenclature for listing a tRNA isodecoder and its
corresponding position? Simply adding the word “position” prior to the last number would distinguish the gene name and the
position in the tRNA of those mapped reads. Alternatively, the data can be split by position, for example using brackets on
the right side of the plot to group all “position 27” rows together.
- line 427–429: these citations are incomplete in presenting what is known about how psi55 influences m1A58. There are
numerous cases known in yeast in which the influence is positive and not negative (Barraud et al 2019, Shaw and Thomas
et al 2024, reviewed in Porat 2025).
- lines 251–252: the meaning of this statement is not clear. Why would a difference in tRNA expression between two
samples cause difficulties in assignment of the modified positions in tRNA?
- Figure 5D: The figure legend describes the plot as a histogram, when 5D is a heatmap. Descriptions for 5D and 5E may
have been swapped in legend.
- Figure 5G: this illustration and legend need to be revised for clarification. There are no arrows being shown, and the
identity of starting and terminal nodes is not clear and thus direction of change. The first two simply have solid lines
connecting the two sites.
The Github link does not work and the GEO accession number states that the data will not be public until 2027. Therefore, it
is not possible to reproduce the analyses with these current circumstances.
